title: Sarah's grave (Genesis 23)
hookLine: Abraham weeps for Sarah and buys a field to bury her

lines: NOT ONE SQUARE FOOT OF LAND.
cards: A funeral home, the morning after. A box of tissues on the desk, and next to it, a price list. Someone is weeping, and someone has to choose a casket, sign forms, decide on a plot.
Grief and paperwork in the same afternoon. Genesis twenty-three is exactly that. Sarah dies at Hebron, a hundred and twenty-seven years old.
And the man who was promised a whole land, who has walked it for years, discovers that he doesn't own a single square foot of it to bury his wife in.

teach.h: TO MOURN FOR SARAH, AND TO WEEP.
teach.b: First, the grief, in the King James Bible: "Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her." The text lets him weep before it lets him do business.

Then he stands up and goes to the Hittites, the people who live there, and he describes himself honestly: "I am a stranger and a sojourner with you." A resident foreigner. After all these years, still a guest.

Give me a place to bury my dead. What follows is a long, polite negotiation in the town gate, and it's worth reading slowly. The Hittites are generous: you're a mighty prince among us, take any of our tombs.
Abraham insists on paying. Ephron, who owns the field with the cave at the end of it, says, I'll give it to you. Abraham says, I'll pay the full price.

teach.h: FOUR HUNDRED SHEKELS, PAID IN FULL.
teach.b: And Ephron, still saying it's nothing between friends, names it: four hundred shekels of silver. Abraham weighs out the silver in front of everyone, and the field and the cave of Machpelah become his.

teach.h: THE LAND HE OWNS IS A GRAVE.
teach.b: After all those promises of land, what Abraham finally owns is a grave. Not a farm. Not a city.

A cave to bury the woman he loved. Later, Abraham himself will be buried there, then Isaac and Rebekah, then Jacob and Leah. Tradition places the cave in Hebron, where Jews, Christians and Muslims still honor it.
Abraham didn't skip the weeping, and he didn't skip the ground.

teach.h: HE GAVE HIS GRIEF A PLACE.
teach.b: He gave his grief a place.

how: Christians bury and remember their dead with funerals, graveside prayers and, in many churches, All Souls' Day or a memorial Sunday each year, when families visit and tend graves.

games.q: you're Abraham. the people of the land offer you any of their tombs for free. what do you do?
o: insist on paying the full price.
games.why: he weighs out four hundred shekels of silver in front of everyone. the field and cave become his, legally, for good.

practice: Think of someone you've lost, whose grave you know, or who has none you can visit, and picture the place where they rest, or where you feel closest to them.
Let whatever comes be there, grief, love, guilt, gratitude; there's no right feeling. If you pray, you can pray for them, or give thanks for them.

wordCard.voice: Sarah's grave. The cave of Machpelah in Hebron, bought for four hundred shekels: the ground Abraham owns in the promised land is a grave.

orig.note: Hebrew: Machpelah, the cave where Sarah, and later Abraham, were buried.

carryVoice: Your line: grief deserves ground. Weeping first, then a place to rest. Day three hundred fifty-eight, done.
